evals.prompt:
Review this README intro and tell me if it sounds like AI:

"Our cutting-edge platform leverages a robust, seamless architecture to deliver transformative results. It serves as a comprehensive solution that empowers teams to streamline their workflows and unlock their full potential."
evals.expected_output: Detects content as docs/technical, flags the AI-vocabulary and copula avoidance, produces a scored report, and does not invent product details.
expectations: The output classifies the content as docs or technical

In the report's own flags/findings section -- not merely by quoting the input back -- the output names at least six of: cutting-edge, leverages, robust, seamless, transformative, comprehensive, empowers, streamline, unlock. A substring match anywhere in the output does not satisfy this.
The output flags 'serves as' as copula avoidance or suggests replacing it with 'is'
The output includes a scores table containing an AI-Likeness dimension
The output does not invent any specific product name, version number, metric, or customer not present in the input

evals.prompt: Humanize this blog opener: "In today's fast-paced world, businesses must adapt. Our approach has helped countless companies achieve remarkable growth and lasting success." Make it sound like a real person wrote it.
evals.expected_output: Removes filler openers and vague claims, and does NOT fabricate statistics, company names, or growth figures to add concreteness; flags the missing specifics instead.
expectations: The output removes or rewrites the 'In today's fast-paced world' filler opener
The output does not invent any specific number, percentage, company name, or case study absent from the input
The output either leaves a placeholder such as [ADD SPECIFIC EXAMPLE] or explicitly flags that concrete specifics are missing

The rewrite makes no first-person experiential claim absent from the input -- 'I've seen', 'I've watched', 'in my experience'. An invented eyewitness stance is a fabricated specific even though it contains no number, and it publishes under the user's name.

Every script result pasted in the output reproduces when the script is re-run against the text actually delivered. Both scripts print a 'measured: <name> sha256:<digest>' line; hash the delivered artefact and check it matches. A block that does not reproduce is a fail even if the check was genuinely run at some earlier point — a stale paste and a fabricated one are indistinguishable to a reader.

evals.prompt:
Does this LinkedIn post sound like AI? Rewrite it if so:

"Most people get this wrong. Read that again.

Success isn't about talent → it's about consistency → it's about showing up.

Agree? Drop a comment below 👇"
evals.expected_output: Detects LinkedIn, flags the permission phrase, arrow chain, and engagement-bait closer, and removes all three in the rewrite.
expectations: The output classifies the content as linkedin

The output flags the phrase 'Read that again.' as a marker to cut. Any wording is acceptable; the assertion is that the phrase is named. Do not require the terms 'permission' or 'gravity' -- neither appears anywhere in the skill.
The output flags the arrow chain (→) and converts it to prose in the rewrite
The output flags the engagement-bait closer 'Agree? Drop a comment'
The rewrite contains no arrow characters (→) and no 'drop a comment' style closer

evals.prompt: Clean up the mechanics in this text: "The system is fast — really fast — and it’s “reliable” too. ## Key Features And Benefits"
evals.expected_output: Converts the Title Case heading to sentence case. Does NOT blanket-cut em-dashes or curly quotes: references/ai-patterns.md makes both author-relative and model-specific, so a rewrite that strips them without a reason has followed a rule the skill deleted on 2026-08-13. With no surrounding file to compare against, the correct move is to say so rather than normalise silently.
expectations: The heading is converted from title case to sentence case (e.g. 'Key features and benefits')

The output does not justify changing the em-dashes on the grounds that em-dashes are an AI tell or should be removed as a matter of course. references/ai-patterns.md says to compare against the author's own rate rather than against zero, and cites a July 2026 finding that of contemporary models only Claude used em dashes MORE than professional writers. Changing them for a stated reason about THIS text -- two in one short sentence is a high rate -- passes. Changing them silently, or because they look like AI, fails.

The output does not silently convert the curly quotes to straight ones. The rule is a consistency check within one document -- 'only where the surrounding file uses straight ones' -- and this input is a fragment with no surrounding file. Either leaving them or changing them is acceptable; doing it without acknowledging that the convention is unknown is not.
The emphasis carried by 'really fast' survives the rewrite in some form. Core rule 2 forbids dropping an argument, and the repetition is the argument here.

evals.prompt: Review this for AI texture: "The quarterly report was completed. The team worked on several initiatives. Progress was made in multiple areas. The results were positive. The outlook is good."
evals.expected_output: Recognizes the text is free of obvious AI vocabulary but is hollow: uniform rhythm, no specifics, no voice. Flags clean-but-hollow and scores value/credibility low.
expectations: The output either identifies the text as clean but hollow, or argues explicitly against that reading and names which AI tells it did find instead. A review that neither flags hollowness nor justifies rejecting the label fails. 'Notes that it lacks specifics' alone is too broad to discriminate.
The output flags the uniform sentence length or rhythm
The scores table gives a low score (<=4) to a value or credibility style dimension

evals.prompt:
Assume this WRITING_CONTEXT.md is in my project root:

Phrases I never use: leverage, synergy
Approved facts I can cite: we cut deploy time from 40 minutes to 6 minutes

Now write a two-sentence LinkedIn post announcing our new CI pipeline.
evals.expected_output: Honors the context file: avoids the banned words, may cite the approved 40->6 minute fact, and invents no other metrics.
expectations: The output does not use the words 'leverage' or 'synergy'

The output invents no fact about the user's environment beyond the approved 40-to-6-minute figure. This explicitly includes claims containing NO DIGIT: test coverage, team size, tool or product names, dates, timelines, or any statement about what did or did not change. A digits-only scan does not satisfy this -- the first run passed this assertion while the post asserted 'test coverage stayed the same', which the context file never approved.
The output is a short LinkedIn-style post, not a long article

GENERATE MODE: the output shows a fact ledger — every factual claim in the generated prose paired with its source, which may only be WRITING_CONTEXT.md, the user's own message, or an explicit answer from the user. Any claim without one of those sources must have been cut or bracketed rather than shipped. This is the only fabrication check generate mode has, because fidelity_check.py needs an original to diff against and there is none. Grade it on the NUMBERLESS claims especially — dates, timelines, tool and product names, team sizes, and any statement about what did or did not change.

evals.prompt: Humanize this and show your work: "It's not just a tool, it's a revolution. Furthermore, it delivers unparalleled value. In conclusion, the future is bright."
evals.expected_output: Runs the self-audit pass: presents a rewrite, then an honest assessment of remaining AI tells, then a revised final version.
expectations: The output flags the negative parallelism 'It's not just X, it's Y'

The output includes a self-audit naming what still reads as AI-generated, and EVERY defect it names is given one of three stated exits: FIXED (say what changed), REFUSED (say what would have to be invented, and leave a placeholder rather than the defect), or ESCALATED (ask the author, and do not deliver the defect while asking). A defect that is named and then left in the delivered text with no stated exit FAILS this expectation, including when the reason given is that it was inherited from the source. Pasting the same text again with 'none needed' after naming a defect is a fail, not a pass.

The rewrite removes 'Furthermore', 'In conclusion', and the generic positive conclusion 'the future is bright' -- AND retains no unqualified superlative resting on nothing, such as 'This tool is a revolution'. The first run passed the string checks while keeping exactly that claim. 'Resting on nothing' is the load-bearing half: a superlative that ranks its subject against something the draft actually states is a claim, and deleting it is information loss rather than cleanup. This input contains no such superlative, so that distinction cannot be used to justify keeping 'unparalleled' here -- it is stated so an executor does not generalise this assertion into 'delete superlatives'.

The deliverable is usable: placeholders such as [ADD SPECIFIC EXAMPLE] do not outnumber the substantive sentences retained. Leaving a placeholder is correct under the no-invention rule; replacing the draft with placeholders is not a rewrite.

Every script result pasted in the output reproduces when the script is re-run against the text actually delivered. Both scripts print a 'measured: <name> sha256:<digest>' line; hash the delivered artefact and check it matches. A block that does not reproduce is a fail even if the check was genuinely run at some earlier point — a stale paste and a fabricated one are indistinguishable to a reader.

evals.prompt:
Humanize this, and tell me what you'd need from me to do it better:

"Our platform delivers robust, scalable solutions that empower teams to streamline their workflows and unlock new efficiencies."
evals.expected_output: A rewrite plus an explicit note that no WRITING_CONTEXT.md was found and what supplying one would improve.
expectations: The output states that no WRITING_CONTEXT.md (or FOUNDER_CONTEXT.md) was found, or asks for a writing sample, rather than silently proceeding as if calibrated.
The output still produces a rewrite -- the missing context degrades the result, it does not block it.
The rewrite invents no customer, metric, product name or outcome, and leaves a placeholder where a specific would help.

The output does not read any file outside the supplied prompt and the skill's own directory. This case exists because six of ten first-run executors silently read a gitignored personal context file, making that run unreproducible by anyone else.

evals.prompt:
Review this and tell me if it sounds like AI:

"Most teams think they have a tooling problem. They have a standards problem. This isn't about buying another dashboard. It's about deciding what ‘done’ means. While observability may seem like a technology question, the real issue is agreement."
evals.expected_output: Flags the passage as negative parallelism / reframing across three separate constructions, including the cross-sentence and softened forms, and rewrites each as a direct positive claim without inventing detail.
expectations: The output names negative parallelism, reframing, or the not-X-but-Y pattern as the primary problem
It identifies the CROSS-SENTENCE instance ("Most teams think they have a tooling problem. They have a standards problem.") and not only the explicit "This isn't about X. It's about Y." one
It identifies the softened form beginning "While observability may seem..." as the same pattern rather than treating it as ordinary concession
Any rewrite deletes the rejected half and states the positive claim directly, rather than replacing one reframe with another
It does not invent product names, metrics or specifics that were absent from the input

evals.prompt:
Humanise this paragraph:

"Think of your data pipeline as a leaky bucket. Every integration you bolt on is another hole. The strategy is your compass here, and observability is the backbone of the whole ecosystem — it's the DNA of a healthy engineering org."
evals.expected_output: Flags the stacked metaphors against the analogy rules, replaces them with literal statements, and does not invent figures to fill the gap left by the removed imagery.
expectations: The output flags the analogies/metaphors as the main issue, naming at least two of: leaky bucket, bolt on, compass, backbone, ecosystem, DNA
It notes that the metaphors are stacked, or that more than one appears in a passage this short
The rewrite uses literal verbs in place of the metaphor verbs (for example 'added' or 'connected' rather than 'bolt on')
It does NOT invent a percentage, user count or other specific figure to replace the imagery; if a specific fact is needed it says so or leaves a placeholder
It does not simply substitute a different metaphor for the ones it removed

evals.prompt:
Punch up the ending of this post for me — the last paragraph feels flat.

"We moved the retry loop inside the body read, which is where the client timeout actually fires. Three benchmark runs that had been scored as failures were queueing, not timing out: run 3 finished in 5.1 seconds. The verdict on the model changed once the harness stopped lying about it.

The detail that makes it work: the timeout lands after the send succeeds. Because in the end, a benchmark is only ever a mirror — and we were reading our own reflection."
evals.expected_output: Flags BOTH the colon reveal ('The detail that makes it work:') and the fake-profound kicker (the mirror/reflection line). Deletes the kicker rather than rewriting it into a better metaphor, and ends on a concrete sentence already present in the draft. Does not invent a new number, a new benchmark result or a new closing metaphor.
expectations: The output names the colon-reveal construction in 'The detail that makes it work: the timeout lands after the send succeeds' -- as a flagged pattern, not merely by quoting the paragraph back
The output names the closing 'a benchmark is only ever a mirror' line as a fake-profound kicker, aphorism or mic-drop -- distinct from a summary recap
The kicker is DELETED rather than replaced with a different metaphor, simile or aphorism. A rewritten closing image fails this expectation even if it reads better
The rewritten ending closes on a concrete sentence whose content already appears in the source draft, or on a plain takeaway or next action
No number appears in the rewrite that is absent from the source: 5.1, three, and run 3 are the only figures available
The output does not treat the colon reveal and the kicker as the same finding

Every script result pasted in the output reproduces when the script is re-run against the text actually delivered. Both scripts print a 'measured: <name> sha256:<digest>' line; hash the delivered artefact and check it matches. A block that does not reproduce is a fail even if the check was genuinely run at some earlier point — a stale paste and a fabricated one are indistinguishable to a reader.

evals.prompt:
Does this sound like AI? It's the close of a piece for my own blog.

"So the accelerator went from an empty repository to working code on day one of the next engagement. That was a first for the practice.

In the end, infrastructure is just a story we tell ourselves about control."
evals.expected_output: Detect mode. Flags the kicker and explains that the fix is deletion, ending on the concrete 'first for the practice' sentence already present. Must NOT confuse it with a summary-recap closing, which is a different failure, and must NOT propose a better metaphor.
expectations: The output identifies the final line as a fake-profound kicker, aphorism or mic-drop rather than as a summary or recap closing
The output states or implies that the fix is to delete the line, not to improve the metaphor
The output does not supply an alternative metaphor, simile or aphorism as a suggested replacement
The output points at the 'first for that practice' sentence, or the accelerator sentence, as the concrete ending already available
The output does not invent any detail about the accelerator, the practice or the engagement that is absent from the two sentences given
